extracted.intended_audience: writers, students, and general readers studying narrative, plot theory, and storytelling
extracted.subtask_description: Conceptual and practical criteria for understanding and constructing plot in fiction, film, and other narratives, including definitions, structural models (e.g., Freytag, three-act), plot devices, and guidance for outlines and summaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot as cause-and-effect relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot is the mapping of events in which each one (except the final) affects at least one other; Forster: 'The king died, and then the queen died of grief' is a plot (cause-and-effect), while 'The king died, and then the queen died' is only a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasises causal linkage between events: select events that have consequences within the narrative. Plot highlights important points which have consequences within the story, in the narrative sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include only major events that move the action
rubrics_metrics.description: A plot does not include memorable scenes that do not relate directly to other events but only 'major events that move the action in a narrative.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude scenes that are vivid or memorable but do not influence subsequent events (examples: Rose spreading her arms on Titanic; Han Solo frozen in carbonite). Focus plot on incidents that change outcomes or cause other events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fabula versus syuzhet (chronology vs discourse ordering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fabula is the chronology of events (what happened); syuzhet is the selection and ordering of those events (the plot thread or discourse sequence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Syuzhet may pick fabula events in non-chronological order to achieve effects (e.g., ⟨a5,a1,a3⟩). Use ordering deliberately to shape perception and emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamiliarization / 'making strange' (Shklovsky)
rubrics_metrics.description: The syuzhet can 'defamiliarize' the fabula — upending familiar presentation, slowing perception, and making the story appear unfamiliar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques: temporal displacements, digressions, placing effects before causes (e.g., Tristram Shandy). Use these to alter reader reconstruction of events and produce stylistic effects, but be mindful of clarity and purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three‑act structure: set-up, confrontation, resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: A common plot structure used in film and Western publishing: Act I (set-up), Act II (confrontation), Act III (resolution), connected by two major plot points/turning points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used frequently in treatments and synopses when selling scripts; acts should be linked by turning points that propel the protagonist between stages. Structure may vary by genre or cultural tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freytag's pyramid — Exposition / Introduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduction/exposition fixes the setting in place and time, sets mood, and introduces characters. Backstory may be alluded to and exposition can be conveyed via dialogues, flashbacks, asides, background details, or narrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use exposition to orient readers without dumping irrelevant detail; introduce only necessary backstory and world details that will affect later events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freytag's pyramid — Rising action (Rise)
rubrics_metrics.description: An exciting force begins after the exposition and builds rising action in stages toward the point of greatest interest; these events are generally the most important parts of the story since the entire plot depends on them to set up the climax and resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange escalating stakes and causal complications that make the climax necessary and probable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freytag's pyramid — Climax (turning point)
rubrics_metrics.description: The climax is the turning point that changes the protagonist's fate; it reveals hidden weaknesses or strengths and determines whether the outcome will be tragic or comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the climax is earned by prior events and that it meaningfully alters the protagonist's trajectory; avoid anticlimax by proper build-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freytag's pyramid — Falling action / Return
rubrics_metrics.description: During the Return, the counter-party's hostility beats upon the hero; Freytag prescribes limiting characters and having fewer falling-action scenes than in the rising movement. Falling action may contain a moment of final suspense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreshadow any catastrophe so it does not appear as a non sequitur; use falling action to resolve consequences but keep the scene count economical compared to the rise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freytag's pyramid — Catastrophe / Denouement
rubrics_metrics.description: The catastrophe or denouement comprises events from the end of the falling action to the actual ending scene where conflicts are resolved. The hero meets his logical destruction in tragedy; denouement unties the 'knot'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unravel complexities to create closure and catharsis. Freytag warns writers not to spare the logical outcome for the hero when appropriate to the drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freytag's three crises (exciting, tragic, final suspense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Freytag extends the five parts with three moments or crises: the exciting force (leads to rising action), the tragic force (leads to falling action), and the force of final suspense (leads to catastrophe).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exciting force is considered necessary; the tragic force and final suspense are optional — use as needed to shape emotional contour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot devices vs dramatic technique
rubrics_metrics.description: A plot device is a means of advancing the plot (motivating characters, creating urgency, resolving difficulties). This contrasts with dramatic technique, where characters take action for well-developed reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious of cheap plot devices (e.g., deus ex machina); prefer actions arising from character motivation (dramatic technique). Familiar plot devices: deus ex machina, MacGuffin, red herring, Chekhov's gun.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot outline: list of scenes and backbone of cause-and-effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A plot outline is a prose telling of a story (often a 'one page') listing scenes; scenes include events, character(s), and setting. In fiction the outline is a rough sketch mapping cause and effect to create a 'solid backbone and structure.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use outlines/roughs/storyboards to check scene order, suspense build, points of view, camera angles/positions (in comics/film), and to serve as a basis for more detailed stages (pencil, screenplay).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot outline goals for comics/visual storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Roughs lay out the flow of panels across a page, ensure the story successfully builds suspense, work out points of view, camera angles, and character positions within panels, and serve as a basis for the next development stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize visual continuity, pacing across pages, and panel composition that supports the causal progression and emotional beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot summary conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: A plot summary is a brief description that explains what happens; it should refer to the author and title and is usually no more than a paragraph long while summarizing the main points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep summaries concise, focus on main events and outcomes, and avoid extraneous scene-level detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: A-Plot (primary driving plotline)
rubrics_metrics.description: An A-Plot refers to the plotline that drives the story — the line that forces most of the action (not necessarily the 'most important' by theme).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the A-Plot to orient supporting subplots (B- and C-plots) so they reinforce or contrast with the main action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot is composed of significant events with consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot is built of significant events in a given story — significant because they have important consequences; 'Plot is the things characters do, feel, think or say, that make a difference to what comes afterward.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing or editing, filter out incidents that do not change state or lead to other events; prioritize causally effective moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversals and recognitions (Aristotelian criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle highlighted two scene types: reversal (peripeteia) which throws action in a new direction, and recognition (anagnorisis) where the protagonist has an important revelation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up reversals as necessary and probable consequences of earlier events; use recognition to alter understanding and deepen stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action and moral/affective purpose (Aristotle)
rubrics_metrics.description: A whole should have a beginning, middle, and end; the action should teach a moral reinforced by emotions (pity, fear, suffering); Aristotle opposed episodic plots and character-centric unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a single unified action that produces coherent emotional and moral effects; avoid disjointed episodic sequences without causal unity.
